newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Renault under attack on plant closure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Renault under attack on plant closure.

text.p: Political pressure mounted on Renault SA on Wednesday as the European Commission gave tacit support to a Belgian plan to sue the French car maker over job losses at its plant near Brussels.
In Paris, French President Jacques Chirac was said to be shocked by the company's methods in closing its Vilvoorde plant in Belgium with the loss of over 3,000 jobs.
Chirac's prime minister, Alain Juppe, was due to hold talks with Renault head Louis Schweitzer on Wednesday.

Last week's abrupt announcement that Vilvoorde would be shut down in June, was swiftly followed by news that the 46 percent state-owned Renault was to axe another 2,700 jobs in France as it grapples with big losses, a price war and shrinking demand.
European Commission President Jacques Santer criticised the Belgian closure and said Renault had not followed the spirit of EU laws in how it went about shutting it down.
"Mr Santer regrets the way in which Renault has managed the closure," said his spokesman, Nikolaus van der Pas. "The spirit of the law was not respected."
Asked by reporters if the Commission thought Renault had a case to answer, van der Pas said: "You can take that as encouragement."
The Belgian federal and Flanders regional governments have threatened to take Renault to court for allegedly failing to respect European labour laws over the closure.

Van der Pas stressed it was not up to the Commission -- the EU's executive body -- to take Renault to court because if the French firm had broken any laws it would be for national governments or trade unions to pursue the matter.
The restructuring has caused anger and dismay in Belgium and prompted nationwide calls for a boycott of French-made products.

Several hundred Renault workers from the doomed Belgian plant drove into northern France on Wednesday on 20 buses to picket a Renault factory at Douai, south of Lille, while French trade unions declared solidarity with their Belgian comrades.

In Vilvoorde, just north of Brussels, shops closed, cars halted and schoolchildren stood still in a five-minute protest against the lost jobs. "This is a massacre for the people," one local told Belgian television.
Renault unions have called a one-hour protest strike on Friday in all plants in France, Belgium and Spain.
The bishopric of Vlaams-Brabant and Mechelen, which covers the Vilvoorde plant, decried the "overriding principle of profit and competitiveness" which motivated such economic decisions.

Renault's embattled chairman did receive some support, with French Industry Minister Franck Borotra backing the restructuring, but distancing the government from blame by saying responsibility for the closure lay with Renault alone.
In a radio interview, Borotra acknowledged that Renault had told the French and Belgian governments of its decision to shut the Vilvoorde plant a few days before the official announcement.
"The chairman of Renault takes responsibility for his decision," Borotra told Europe 1 radio, adding that the move was needed to reduce costs and respond to competition.
But he also said the company had an obligation to limit the human cost of its reorganisation to a minimum.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who has bitterly attacked the Renault move, also said he had been told of the impending cuts a few days before they were made public.
In an angry gesture, the Belgian government on Tuesday cancelled an order for 150 Renault Megane cars.
Concern over Renault's decision runs deeper than just a local row between two EU neighbours, raising the issue of cross-border investment policies within the Union.
Belgian media have implied that Renault flouted the spirit of EU labour laws by sacrificing Belgian staff at a modern plant in order to save less efficient French jobs at home.
French Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin has also warned that the Vilvoorde job losses, Renault's biggest cuts in five years, could tarnish France's social image in Europe.
